newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan investors barely change portfolios for May.
newsitem.headline: Japan investors barely change portfolios for May.

text.p: Japanese institutional investors plan to increase the weighting of cash holdings slightly in May but their portfolio plans remain essentially the same as the previous month, a Reuters investment survey showed on Friday.
Although investors said worrisome factors exist in each of the major financial markets, they do not expect any significant disruptions in May, with markets expected to move in a narrow range.
The average overall weighting of cash holdings rose 0.67 percentage point from the previous survey to 15.67 percent.
For bonds, the average overall portfolio weighting fell to 39.33 percent, down 0.09 percentage point, and the average overall weighting of equities was 0.58 point lower at 45.00 percent.
The Reuters monthly Global Asset Allocation survey asked 16 Japan-based financial institutions in late April about their investment strategies for May.
Within the equities portfolio, the weighting of shares in Japanese, German and some other European markets rose while the weighting of U.S. and British shares fell.

The weighting of Japanese equities showed a particularly large increase, helped by a slightly more optimistic outlook on Japan's economic recovery, a rebound in corporate profits and an influx of pension fund investment into stocks.

But some investors said lingering worries over Japan's financial system, which is burdened by problem loans, were dampening sentiment, while a scandal at leading brokerage Nomura Securities Co Ltd was undermining market credibility.

Nomura has said that two of its directors were involved in suspected illegal deals in which substantial sums of Nomura money were moved to the account of a corporate customer who media reports linked to a racketeer.
Investors surveyed said economic indicators in May are also expected to show the negative effects of April's consumption tax increase.
The question of whether the U.S. Federal Reserve Board will raise interest rates at the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on May 20 was the biggest concern for the U.S. stock market.
Most of those surveyed expected a rate rise and said an increase of about 0.25 percentage point had already been factored in by the markets, the survey said.
Other factors that may dampen U.S. equities include a slowdown in capital inflows from equities trust funds and currency movements affected by trade tensions between Japan and the United States.
An optimistic outlook for U.S. corporate profits was, however, cited as a positive factor.
European markets were expected to follow developments in the United States.
Investors said they thought it best to keep investments spread over different countries.
Nikko Research said low interest rates and better corporate profits made the German market attractive, with room to move higher barring any sudden confusion in the U.S. market.
The weighting for other continental European markets rose for the first time in four months to 7.51 percent, its highest level since the survey began in June 1994.
"France and Britain are about to have elections but continental European markets are the most attractive of the world's markets," said Daiwa Research.
In bond markets, the weighting for the Japan market dropped, while the weighting for the U.S. market also fell over concerns about rising rates.
The Japan market weighting slipped 0.73 point to 13.91 percent, its first time below 14 percent since the survey began.
Investors said they could not get too excited about the Japanese market due to concerns that prices were moving at the top of their range and the Bank of Japan may raise interest rates.
Most said they expected a rate rise in the summer, although they expected the central bank not to move for some months after the sales tax was increased on April 1 to five percent from three percent.
In Europe, the weighting for France fell, but there were rises for other European markets, with the German bond market seen as particularly attractive.
"It doesn't look like the mark is going to weaken in the near future and it's also difficult to see the economy getting better, so German bonds have merit," said Okasan Economic Research.
